user_text: Hello there. My grandson put this on the tablet for me and says I'm to tell it things, so here goes.
I drove buses in Cork for thirty-one years before I retired. These days I keep bees at the bottom of the garden.
My grandson is Cillian. He's 16 and can fix anything with a screen, which is how you and I have come to be acquainted.
The honey goes to a little shop on the quay called Dandelion Pantry. The woman who runs it, Agnes, pays me in scones about as often as in money.
If the summer is kind I might split the hives, though I said that last year and the year before.
Cillian's mother is my daughter Deirdre, a nurse up at Clonmore Hospital, and she worries about me far more than she needs to.
That's plenty for one evening. Goodnight to you.
Good afternoon. Wet and blowy today. Cillian called round after school; he's taken up the guitar, heaven help us all.
I told you wrong about Cillian. He's 17, not 16. He had his birthday in April and I still count him younger than he is.
My late wife's sister Bernadette rings me every Sunday from Boston, regular as the tide.
I've half a mind to enter a jar in the county show this year and see what the judges make of it.
What did I say the shop that takes my honey is called? I'm writing new labels.
Where does my daughter work? The name's gone clean out of my head and I want to drop in a flask of soup.
Morning. The sun's out and so are the bees.
How old is my grandson now? I want the right number on his card.
Who runs Dandelion Pantry, again? A neighbour asked and I couldn't bring the woman's name to mind.
My daughter is a nurse, isn't she? The man at the chemist asked and I found myself doubting it.
Which ward is my daughter on? I'd like to send a tin of biscuits to the whole team.
Could you help me write a short blurb for the honey jars? Something homely, not too fancy.
What's Agnes's surname? I'd like to send her a proper card at Christmas.
